dok_rationale: Part (c) coordinates the lower-tail p-value, preset threshold, asymmetric decision logic, and SRS population scope to adjudicate two conclusions and trace the consequence of overclaiming.
stem: Suppose a help desk closed 1,200 tickets in a quarter. To investigate whether their population mean resolution time was below 12 hours, an analyst took an SRS of 24 and used $\alpha=0.05$.\par\smallskip \textbf{Leah:} ``The lower-tail test gives $t=-1.5747$, $df=23$, and $p\approx0.0645$. I would state what evidence this does and does not provide.''\par \textbf{Damon:} ``Because $p>0.05$, accept $H_0$. The test proves the population mean was exactly 12 hours and the observed difference was only chance.''
first_take: Which account is more defensible? Cite the p-value comparison or a claim that a test can or cannot justify.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Define the population mean and state hypotheses for the research question.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Verify random, 10 percent, and shape conditions. Compute $SE$, $t$, $df$, and the lower-tail p-value; interpret the p-value.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Adjudicate the accounts. Compare $p$ with $\alpha$, distinguish the formal decision from acceptance or proof, state the scoped population conclusion, and explain the two beliefs produced by the rejected account.

answers.a: Let $\mu$ be the mean resolution time for all 1,200 tickets closed that quarter. $H_0:\mu=12$ hours and $H_a:\mu<12$ hours.
answers.b: The SRS satisfies $24\leq0.10(1{,}200)=120$; the symmetric, outlier-free sample supports shape for $n=24$. $SE=2.8/\sqrt{24}=0.57155$, so $t=(11.1-12)/0.57155=-1.57467$, $df=23$, and $p=0.06449$. If $\mu=12$, the chance of an SRS result at least this low in the direction of $H_a$ is about 0.0645.
answers.c: Leah is warranted. Since $0.0645>0.05$, fail to reject $H_0$. The sample does not provide convincing evidence that the mean for all 1,200 tickets was below 12 hours. The p-value assumes $\mu=12$; it is not the probability that assumption is true. Failing to reject says the data are not sufficiently incompatible with 12, not that $\mu=12$ was proved. Chance is plausible but not proved to be the only explanation. The rejected account would falsely report both equality and certainty about chance.

expectedElements.description: Distinguishes failure to reject from acceptance or proof
States the 1,200-ticket scope and both false beliefs

scoringGuide.E: Uses the threshold, conditional p-value meaning, scoped conclusion, and both limits of the rejected account.
scoringGuide.P: Gives the correct decision but incompletely explains p-value meaning, scope, or why equality was not established.
scoringGuide.I: Accepts the null, treats the p-value as a null probability, or concludes the mean equals 12.
